title: The messianic age
hook: Maimonides pictures the world running as usual, but without war or hunger

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: you can be moses. Nothing written at your birth closes the road. Did your autopilot moment come, and did you choose? Day one thousand one hundred fifty-three.

Sunrise. A baker unlocks the shop. Buses run. Children argue about whose turn it is. Rain falls on schedule, or doesn't. Nothing about the morning looks miraculous. And yet, in this picture, nobody anywhere is marching to war, and nobody anywhere goes to bed hungry. That ordinary-looking morning is close to how Maimonides describes the days of the messiah, in the closing chapters of his law code. Not fire from the sky. Not a new set of physics. The same world, with the worst things gone. Today's word is that picture.
screen: `AN ORDINARY MORNING.` → `NO WAR. NO HUNGER.` → `THE SAME WORLD.`

segments.voice: The messianic age. Maimonides closes the Mishneh Torah with it, in the Laws of Kings. Turn it four ways. First, the world keeps its habits. Don't imagine, he writes, that in the days of the messiah anything of the world's ordinary order will be canceled, or that something new will enter creation. The world goes on in its usual way. He quotes a sage in the Talmud: the only difference between this world and the days of the messiah is that Israel will no longer be subject to the rule of other kingdoms. Second, the wolf and the lamb. Isaiah says, "And the wolf shall dwell with the lamb." Maimonides reads it as a parable: the nations once fierce as wolves will live in peace. Third, he admits what he doesn't know. How all of this will happen, he says, nobody will know until it does. The prophets' words are unclear, and sages disagreed. So he warns readers not to get lost calculating the details. Fourth, what it's for. The sages didn't long for those days, he writes, to rule the world or to eat and drink and celebrate. They longed for them so they would be free to study and to know God, with nothing pressing on them. In that time, he says, there will be no famine and no war, no envy and no rivalry. Good things will be plentiful. And the whole world's occupation will be to know God. He ends the entire code with Isaiah: "for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD, as the waters cover the sea." Jews hold a range of views on the messiah today, and some streams speak more of a messianic age than a person. But this is his picture: ordinary days, made safe.
screen: `THE WORLD KEEPS ITS HABITS.` · `THE WOLF AND THE LAMB, A PARABLE.` · `HOW, NOBODY KNOWS YET.` · `FREE TO KNOW GOD.` · then, large: `AS THE WATERS COVER THE SEA.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe slowly. Bring to mind tomorrow morning where you live. Your street, your kitchen, the people nearby. Now take one thing out of the picture: somebody in your town who is hungry. See the morning without that. Then ask a plain question. What is one step, this week, that moves toward it? A bag of groceries to a food bank. A meal for a neighbor. A recurring gift, even a small one. Choose one and fix a day for it. If you pray, you can hold the words "as the waters cover the sea" for a few breaths. The bell holds the time.
The messianic age. In Maimonides' telling, the world running as it always has, but without war, hunger, envy or rivalry, so that people are free to know God. Today's word.
Your line: the world, at peace. Today, take the step you chose toward a world without hunger, or put it on the calendar with a time. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: The traditional daily prayers ask for redemption, and the Aleinu prayer, said near the end of services, looks toward a world united in knowing God. Some communities connect that hope to feeding the hungry and working for peace now.

original.note: Hebrew: the days of the messiah, the phrase Maimonides uses for the age he describes.

what it means: in Maimonides' picture, the same world, without war, hunger, envy or rivalry.
what a scholar hears: Hilchot Melachim 12, quoting the sage Shmuel from Berakhot 34b, reading Isaiah 11:6 as parable, and ending the code with Isaiah 11:9.
